author: xiaokuerz
title: fix(audio): reset stale fade state when GainNode is reused/reconnected

questions.prompt: ResetFadeState sets fadeInState_ = true but collFadeInState_ = false. Why is one enabled and the other disabled after a reset?

options.text: fadeInState_=true enables a fade-in ramp on reconnect to avoid an audible pop; collFadeInState_=false because there is no active collaborative fade partner to sync with on a fresh reconnect, so coll fade-in should stay off.
It is a typo — both should be true to enable fade-in consistently across primary and collaborative paths.
fadeInState_=true means fade-out is done and fade-in is pending; collFadeInState_=false means the collaborative fade has already finished.
The values are arbitrary — the only thing that matters is that fadeOutState_ and collFadeOutState_ are cleared to NO_FADEOUT.

questions.explanation: fadeInState_ controls the primary fade-in path: setting it to true starts a fade-in ramp so the signal ramps up from zero instead of snapping to full volume (which would produce a pop). collFadeInState_ controls the collaborative fade path: on a fresh reconnect there is no collaborator to coordinate with, so it is set to false to disable collaborative fade-in. Setting it to true would incorrectly trigger a collaborative fade-in ramp without a partner. The asymmetry is intentional, not a typo.
questions.reinforce: Correct — the asymmetry is deliberate: enable primary fade-in to avoid pop, disable collaborative fade-in since there is no partner to sync with.

questions.prompt: If ResetFadeState() were removed from this call site and the reconnected GainNode still had fadeOutState_ = DONE_FADEOUT from a previous Pause, what would happen to audio output?

options.text: SignalProcess would continue silencing every frame, leaving the reused node permanently muted — the exact bug this PR fixes.
ResetVolume() already clears all fade state, so removing ResetFadeState() would have no effect.
The node would crash on the next SignalProcess call because DONE_FADEOUT is an invalid state after reconnect.
The fade-out would automatically restart, producing a brief silence that recovers on its own.

questions.explanation: DONE_FADEOUT is a terminal state — once a fade-out completes, SignalProcess writes zeros to every sample indefinitely. It never self-recovers. ResetVolume() only resets volume-related members (curGain_, etc.), not fade state. Without ResetFadeState(), the stale DONE_FADEOUT persists and the node stays muted forever. This is precisely the bug described in the PR: a reused/reconnected node carries stale DONE_FADEOUT and remains silent.
questions.reinforce: Right — DONE_FADEOUT is terminal, SignalProcess silences every frame, and ResetVolume does not touch fade state.

questions.prompt: Under what condition does the else branch (the reuse path that calls ResetFadeState) execute?

options.text: When a GainNode for this sessionId already exists in idGainMap_ — meaning the node was not erased after a prior disconnect and CreateGainNode is being called again for the same session.
When SafeGetMap fails to find the node and returns a default-constructed empty shared_ptr.
When preNodeInfo contains invalid parameters and a new node cannot be constructed.
Every time CreateGainNode is called — the else branch is the default path.

questions.explanation: SafeGetMap returns the existing shared_ptr from idGainMap_ if a node for sessionId is present. The if (!gainNode) branch creates a new node when the lookup returns null (no existing entry). The else branch runs when gainNode is non-null — i.e., a node already exists in the map for this sessionId. This happens when the node was not erased (e.g., after a Pause that leaves DONE_FADEOUT) and CreateGainNode is called again. The original code used CHECK_AND_RETURN which would silently skip; the new code reuses and resets.
questions.reinforce: Correct — the else branch fires when SafeGetMap finds an existing node, meaning the node survived in the map from a previous lifecycle.

questions.prompt: The test fills inputBuf with UT_UNIT_GAIN (non-zero), then calls SignalProcess with DONE_FADEOUT set. The last sample is 0.0f. What does this verify about SignalProcess's behavior when fadeOutState_ is DONE_FADEOUT?

options.text: SignalProcess sees DONE_FADEOUT and writes zero (silence) to the output buffer, overriding the non-zero input data — this is the bug: the terminal fade state permanently silences audio.
SignalProcess skips processing entirely, leaving the buffer in its original non-zero state — the EXPECT_EQ would then fail, but it does not.
FillBuffer wrote zeros into inputBuf, so the zero output is expected regardless of fade state.
DONE_FADEOUT triggers a fade-in ramp from zero, so only the first frame is zero and the rest are non-zero — but the test checks only the last sample.

questions.explanation: FillBuffer fills the buffer with UT_UNIT_GAIN (a non-zero unit gain value). After SignalProcess, the last sample is 0.0f, proving that SignalProcess actively wrote zeros over the non-zero input when fadeOutState_ is DONE_FADEOUT. This is the core bug: DONE_FADEOUT is a terminal state where the node silences all output indefinitely. If SignalProcess had skipped processing, the buffer would still contain the original non-zero FillBuffer data and the EXPECT_EQ would fail. Option C is wrong because UT_UNIT_GAIN is explicitly non-zero.
questions.reinforce: Exactly — the non-zero input is overwritten with zeros by SignalProcess when DONE_FADEOUT is set, confirming the permanent-silence bug.

questions.prompt: The comment says 'DisConnect erases the node, so reuse is unlikely, but reset for parity/defense.' What does this imply about the relationship between this else branch and the one in HpaeProcessCluster::CreateGainNode?

options.text: In the virtual cluster, DisConnect removes the node from the map, so the else branch rarely fires in practice. The reset is added defensively to mirror HpaeProcessCluster's behavior, guarding against any code path that leaves a stale node in the map despite a disconnect.
The comment means this else branch is dead code and should be removed — it can never execute because DisConnect always erases the node.
DisConnect erases the node only in HpaeProcessCluster, not in HpaeVirtualProcessCluster, so this branch is the primary reuse path for virtual clusters.
The reset is unnecessary because the virtual cluster never uses fade state at all — collFade variables are only meaningful in the physical cluster.

questions.explanation: The comment explicitly states 'reuse is unlikely' because DisConnect erases the node from idGainMap_. However, 'unlikely' does not mean 'impossible' — there may be edge-case code paths (e.g., a device switch without a full disconnect, or a race condition) that leave a stale node. The author chose to add the reset defensively ('for parity/defense') rather than rely on the assumption that the node is always erased. This mirrors the HpaeProcessCluster behavior for consistency. Option B is wrong because 'unlikely' is not 'never' — defensive programming is intentional, not dead code.
questions.reinforce: Correct — the branch is defensive parity, not dead code. 'Unlikely' means guard against edge cases, not that it never fires.

questions.prompt: The test deliberately sets fadeInState_ = false and collFadeInState_ = true — the opposite of what ResetFadeState produces (true and false). Why does the test invert these values before calling ResetFadeState?

options.text: Setting the values to the opposite of the expected output ensures the test would catch a no-op ResetFadeState that fails to write these fields — if the values were already correct, a broken reset would pass the test silently.
false and true are the default constructor values, so the test is just documenting what a fresh node looks like before reset.
The inverted values trigger a fade-out before the reset, which is needed to exercise the full fade state machine.
The test sets them this way because DONE_FADEOUT requires fadeInState_ to be false as a precondition — otherwise the reset would crash.

questions.explanation: This is a fundamental test-design principle: you set up the pre-state to be different from the expected post-state so the test actually verifies that the function wrote the values. If fadeInState_ were already true before ResetFadeState, then EXPECT_EQ(fadeInState_, true) would pass even if ResetFadeState did nothing — a false-positive. By setting it to false first, the test proves ResetFadeState actively wrote true. The same logic applies to collFadeInState_ (set true, expect false). This guards against a regression where someone removes a line from ResetFadeState but the test still passes because the pre-existing value happened to match.
questions.reinforce: Spot on — inverting pre-state vs expected post-state is what makes the test actually verify the write, not just confirm a pre-existing value.
